title: Shurpanakha at the hut
hook: a visitor walks up to the hut at Panchavati and tells Rama to leave his wife for her
carry: eka-patni-vrata: rama's vow of one wife
tomorrow: The wound that starts a war

segments.voice: Yesterday: on a cold dawn walk, Rama stopped Lakshmana from blaming Kaikeyi. Satyam, priyam: speak what's true, and kindly.

The quiet ends the way a lot of trouble starts: with someone noticing someone. Rama sits outside the hut, talking with Sita and Lakshmana, when a rakshasi, a woman of the rakshasa people, comes through the trees and sees him. She stops. She wants him, right then, completely. She walks straight up and asks: who are you, dressed like a hermit but carrying a bow, with a wife beside you, in a forest that belongs to rakshasas?
screen: `SOMEONE NOTICES SOMEONE.` → `A RAKSHASI AT THE HUT.` → `WHO ARE YOU, WITH A BOW?`

segments.voice: Rama answers plainly: his name, his father's, Sita's and Lakshmana's, and why they're in the forest. Then he asks who she is. I am Shurpanakha, she says, sister of Ravana, king of the rakshasas, and of Khara and Dushana, who rule this part of the forest. I saw you and I want you. Be my husband. Leave this woman. Then it turns ugly: she says she'll eat Sita, and Lakshmana too. Her name means she of the nails like winnowing fans. Rama's first answer is simple: I'm married, and my wife is here. Then he laughs and suggests she try his brother, and Lakshmana jokes back. Some readers are uneasy with that teasing; others read it as turning aside a dangerous moment without violence. The text doesn't settle it. But hold on to Rama's first answer, because Hindus have. Rama's own father had three chief queens. Rama keeps one. Tradition calls him eka-patni-vrata, the one vowed to a single wife. Years later in the Ramayana, when a great ritual needs his wife beside him and Sita isn't there, he sets a golden image of her in her place rather than marry again. Here's the teaching under it. Hinduism doesn't call desire bad. Kama, desire and love, is one of the four aims of a good life, beside dharma, artha and moksha. But kama is meant to run inside dharma, like a river inside its banks. Shurpanakha is desire with no banks: I want you, so leave her. Rama is desire kept by a vow. That's why many Hindu elders bless a new couple to be like Rama and Sita.
screen: `I AM SHURPANAKHA. BE MY HUSBAND.` · `I'M MARRIED. THE BROTHERS JOKE.` · `ONE WIFE, ONE VOW.` · `A GOLDEN IMAGE, NOT A NEW WIFE.` · then, large: `EKA-PATNI-VRATA: DESIRE KEPT BY A VOW.`

segments.voice: If there's a picture of Rama and Sita in your home, or a photo of two people you love who kept their promise to each other, look at it for this sit. Notice what held them together: the love, and the vow around it. Breathe slowly. If nothing like that is near, picture a couple you admire and silently wish them well.
Shurpanakha. Ravana's sister, she of the nails like winnowing fans, who sees Rama and demands he marry her.
Hold on to it: eka-patni-vrata, Rama's vow of one wife, desire kept inside dharma. Tomorrow, the jokes run out. That's day five hundred sixty-one.

fork.setup: someone powerful tells a married man: leave your wife, i'm better. by Rama's example, what fits?
options: say it plainly: i'm married, and my wife is here.
keep it vague, so nobody gets angry.

fork.reveal: Rama's first word is the plain truth: i'm married. tradition calls him eka-patni-vrata, vowed to one wife, though his father had three chief queens.

original.note: Sanskrit śūrpaṇakhā: śūrpa (winnowing basket) + nakha (nail): she of the nails like winnowing fans.

chat.meaning: When Shurpanakha told Rama to leave Sita, he answered: I'm married. Tradition calls him eka-patni-vrata, so calling a couple Ram-Sita wishes them love kept inside a promise.

tie.story: When Ravana's sister told Rama to leave Sita and marry her, Rama answered first: I'm married, and my wife is here.

rakshasi.meaning: a woman of the rakshasa people

Khara.meaning: her brother, who rules this part of the forest

eka-patni-vrata.meaning: vowed to a single wife, a traditional title of Rama

kama.meaning: desire and love, one of the four aims of life

recall: a religious fast, kept as a vow
